items.speaker: Rt Hon CHRIS HIPKINS
items.text: Point of order, Madam
Speaker. Thank you, Madam Speaker. When Ministers give incorrect information in
answers to oral questions, there is an onus on them to come back to the House and do
what David Seymour has just done and stating that they gave incorrect information, but
there is also an onus on them to provide the correct information.
David Seymour has just made it clear to the House that he provided incorrect
information, but he hasn’t done the second part of that, which is to discharge his
responsibility for correcting incorrect information, and it is to provide what the correct
information actually is. He has indicated that the Fire Service were disrupted mor e than
once by having faulty equipment in responding to calls, but he hasn’t told us how many
times.

items.speaker: DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: Thank you. Does the Minister have the answer on hand? If not,
the possibility is either now or at the earliest opportunity.

items.speaker: Hon DAVID SEYMOUR
items.text: Well, I’m sorry, but the Leader
of the Opposition’s assertion is incorrect. You do have an obligation to address questions,
which I did at the time, and to correct any incorrect information, which I have. There’s
no further obligation.

items.speaker: Rt Hon CHRIS HIPKINS
items.text: Point of order, Madam
Speaker. David Seymour sought leave to correct an answer, and, on that basis, the House
unanimously gave him leave to do so. He didn’t seek leave to withdraw information; he
sought leave to correct information. He has not done that.

items.speaker: DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: The advice I have is that if the Minister knows the answer, he
should give it to the Hou se, and if he doesn’t, he should give it to the House as soon as
possible.

items.speaker: Hon DAVID SEYMOUR
items.text: Well, with the greatest of
respect, the problem is that th ere may not always be an answer. Therefore, you can’t
always be—that’s why you’re required to address the question; not answer it.

items.speaker: Rt Hon CHRIS HIPKINS
items.text: Point of order, Madam
Speaker. If the Minister does not know the answer, then how would he have corrected the
answer? He must know the answer; therefore, he is obliged to tell the House what the
answer is, given that the previous answer he gave was incorrect.

items.speaker: Hon DAVID SEYMOUR
items.text: I just really hope that this is not
how Labour Party logic works every day, because the simple fact is that while the
statement made has been advised—[Interruption]

items.speaker: DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: Quiet—the Minister is speaking.

items.speaker: Hon DAVID SEYMOUR
items.text: —to be incorrect, that does not mean that a correct answer
is available. It may be that the answer giv en was simply erroneous. That’s why it has
being withdrawn, and with the incorrect part removed, the answer is now correct.

items.speaker: DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: The Minister is saying that he doesn’t have an answer
available—

items.speaker: Hon David Seymour
items.text: You guys are simple.

items.speaker: DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: —so, yeah.

items.speaker: Hon David Seymour
items.text: Simple, simple.

items.speaker: Rt Hon CHRIS HIPKINS
items.text: Point of order, Madam
Speaker. That isn’t what he’s saying; he appears to be saying he’s not willing to give it.
If he—
13822 Points of Order 4 Nov 2025

items.speaker: DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: No, that’s not what I heard. I heard him say—

items.speaker: Hon David Seymour
items.text: Simple man.

items.speaker: DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: —there wasn’t an answer available. That is what he just said
to the House.

items.speaker: Rt Hon CHRIS HIPKINS
items.text: A further point of order,
Madam Speaker. If it, therefore, becomes clear that David Seymour has been advised
what the number is and he has chosen not to give that information to the House, will he
still be in breach of the House, as he would have been had he not corrected it?

items.speaker: Hon DAVID SEYMOUR
items.text: Speaking to the point of order,
maybe I can help the member out. I’ve been advised t hat a number is not currently
available, so therefore it’s not possible to answer the question —which is what I’ve been
trying to get through to the simple man over there this whole time.

items.speaker: DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: Yeah, that’s fine. There’s currently—

items.speaker: Rt Hon Chris Hipkins
items.text: A further point of order, Madam Speaker.

items.speaker: DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: I’m accepting that there’s not currently an answer available
that the Minister has at this point in time—

items.speaker: Rt Hon Chris Hipkins
items.text: Yep, I’m accepting that, too.

items.speaker: DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: That’s what he said.

items.speaker: Rt Hon CHRIS HIPKINS
items.text: Madam Speaker, you’ll note
that this is a serious matter, where a Minister has to seek leave to correct an answer in
order to not breach the privileges of the House. I have raised the issue with you correctly
and appropriately.

items.speaker: DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: Yes.

items.speaker: Rt Hon CHRIS HIPKINS
items.text: I haven’t insulted the Minister.

items.speaker: DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: No.

items.speaker: Rt Hon CHRIS HIPKINS
items.text: Multiple times in his answers to that, he chose to insult
me and attack me in breach of the rules of the House. What would the consequence of
that be for him?

items.speaker: DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: Look, I will follow up and have a look at the Hansard because
I didn’t pick up an insult. I know there was a bit of to -ing and fro-ing coming from the
Minister, but I didn’t pick up the insult, and so I will look at the Hansard and I will come
back to you.
Question No. 1—Prime Minister
1. Rt Hon CHRIS HIPKINS (Leader of the Opposition) to the Prime Minister:
Does he stand by all his Government’s statements and actions?

items.speaker: Rt Hon CHRISTOPHER LUXON
items.text: Yes.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Chris Hipkins
items.text: If the economy has turned the corner, as he’s repeatedly
claimed, why have record numbers of New Zealanders been applying for KiwiSaver
hardship withdrawals in the past 12 months?

items.speaker: Rt Hon CHRISTOPHER LUXON
items.text: Well, as I’ve explained to the member before,
it’s no doubt been a very challenging time for the New Zealand economy. The previous
Government drove up spending, inflation, an d interest rates, and put the economy into
recession, and people lose their jobs as a consequence of that. But there are good signs.
It’s good to see that job ads are up 3.5 percent. It’s good to see that building consents are
up 12 percent just in the last quarter.
4 Nov 2025 Oral Questions 13823

items.speaker: Rt Hon Chris Hipkins
items.text: Is he aware that under his leadership, hardship withdrawals
from KiwiSaver have outnumbered first-home withdrawals from KiwiSaver month after
month, when previously it only happened once in 10 years?

items.speaker: Rt Hon CHRISTOPHER LUXON
items.text: Well, as I said to the member in my answer to
his first question, it has been a difficult time for the New Zealand economy. We inherited
a recession that was probably the worst in 35 years. There was a long COVID hangover,
thanks to the previous Government being the second - biggest-spending Government in
the Western world —spending $66 billion that no one seems to know where it went to.
The reality, though, is that things are getting better: exports are up 4 percent; interest rates
are down 300 basis points.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Chris Hipkins
items.text: Has increasing the cost of doctors visits, home insurance,
public transport, car registration, the price of going to a pharmacy, and student loans
during a cost of living crisis made things better or worse for everyday Kiwi families?

items.speaker: Rt Hon CHRISTOPHER LUXON
items.text: Well, I acknowledge that many of those things
that drive inflation, and particularly electricity but also, most importantly, council rates—
that member opposes council rates. If he wanted to tackle that problem, he would come
on board with the Government’s initiative to put a cap on rates.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Chris Hipkins
items.text: Is the Government considering a law change to ban homeless
people from central business districts; if so, why?

items.speaker: Rt Hon CHRISTOPHER LUXON
items.text: Our Government is doing everything we can to
support people who are in homeless situations, and that’s why you’ve seen 300 mo re
places made available through Housing First. A hundred of those 300 homes and
accommodation have already been built, with 200 in Auckland, but, of course, our
Government and our Ministers will work with lots of people to see what we can do.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Chris Hipkins
items.text: Point of order, Madam Speaker. It was a very straightforward
question: is the Government considering a law change to ban homeless people from
central business districts; if so, why? I didn’t ask the Prime Minister what does  he think
about homelessness; I asked him specifically whether they’re considering a change to the
law to ban homeless people from CBDs.

items.speaker: DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: The Prime Minister did say that the Government will do what
they can. I would like to know if the Prime Minister could elaborate on that to answer
that specific part of the question.

items.speaker: Rt Hon CHRISTOPHER LUXON
items.text: I’m quite comfortable that I’ve answered one of
those legs of those two legs in that question.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Chris Hipkins
items.text: Is the Government considering a law change to ban homeless
people from central business districts?

items.speaker: Rt Hon CHRISTOPHER LUXON
items.text: There have been no Cabinet decisions or
discussion on that topic.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Chris Hipkins
items.text: Has the Cabinet discussed a law change to ban homeless
people from central business districts?

items.speaker: Rt Hon CHRISTOPHER LUXON
items.text: In answer to the answer I just gave the member
for his last question, no.
Chlöe Swarbrick: When, if ever, will the Prime Minister finally respond to my many
invitations to walk the streets of Auckland Central and meet the people, including the
children, who his Government’s policies have made homeless?

items.speaker: Rt Hon CHRISTOPHER LUXON
items.text: Well, no disrespect to the member, but when she
was part of a Labour-Greens Government and had one of her members as the Minister for
homelessness, we saw $1 billion spent on emergency housing and a 37 percent increase
in homelessness. This Government’s record on housing, I would line up against Labour,
Greens, and Te Pāti Māori any day of the week. The great Labour Prime Ministers of their
era must be rolling in their graves with the legacy of Labour and Greens housing—
13824 Oral Questions 4 Nov 2025

items.speaker: DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: OK, that’s enough.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Chris Hipkins
items.text: If booting people out of emergency accommodation has fixed
the homelessness problem, why is the Government now considering changing the law to
ban homeless people?

items.speaker: Rt Hon CHRISTOPHER LUXON
items.text: Well, I reject the characterisation of that
question, because here’s the deal on housing: this Government has delivered housing
affordability for people who want to purchase a hou se or to rent a house. This is the
Government that took 6,000 people off the State house wait -list while that member
increased it fourfold over six years, this is the Government that took 3,200 households
out of emergency housing, and this is the Government that is doing a lot to help homeless
support.

items.speaker: Hon Shane Jones
items.text: Supplementary.

items.speaker: DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: Is this—[Interruption] Quiet, please. Is this a supplementary
question, Minister Jones?

items.speaker: Hon Shane Jones
items.text: Correct. To the Prime Minister, is the Prime Minister aware that a
capital gains tax leads to complications, complexity, and administrative dead weight?

items.speaker: DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: It’s not—well, it is relevant to the lead question, so I’ll let the
Prime Minister answer that.

items.speaker: Rt Hon CHRISTOPHER LUXON
items.text: Well, I thank the member for raising that issue
because I’m saying that taxing Kiwis and their houses and their KiwiSaver accounts is
not the way forward to help people with the cost of living. It’s just adding cost and adding
tax. On this side of the House, we believe in low taxes. We believe in backing people who
want to make something happen, and not in taxing everybody in sight. [Interruption]

items.speaker: DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: Question—quiet during questions, please.
Question No. 2—Finance
2. CAMERON BREWER (National—Upper Harbour) to the Minister of Finance:
What is the Government’s revenue strategy?
Hon SIMON WATTS (Minister of Revenue) on behalf of the Minister of Finance:
A revenue strategy is required by the Public Finance  Act. The current Government
strategy, part of the 2025 Fiscal Strategy Report, states that a good tax system is one that,
among other things, “finances public expenditure in a fair and efficient way”, “encourages
effort and investment”, and “has low compliance and administrative costs”. It goes on to
say, “The Government will operate a stable, predictable revenue system”, and it adds that
the Government “is committed to public engagement in the design of tax policy”.

items.speaker: Cameron Brewer
items.text: What does the strategy say about future revenue and expenses?

items.speaker: Hon SIMON WATTS
items.text: On behalf of the Minister of Finance, the strategy recognises
that Government spending is currently greater than revenue, meaning the operating
balance is in deficit. Revenue and spending need to be brought back into balance.
Crucially, the strategy states that “Spending restraint is the Government’s primary lever
for achieving these goals. With prudent control of spending, the Government does not
intend to seek”—nor does it need to seek—“major additional sources of revenue.” I would
also note that a tax increase announced alongside spending increases that it matches dollar
for dollar does absolutely nothing to improve the operating deficit or Government debt.

items.speaker: Cameron Brewer
items.text: What has the Government done to encourage effort and investment
through the tax system?

items.speaker: Hon SIMON WATTS
items.text: On behalf of the Minister of Finance: in last year’s Budget,
the Government increased personal income  tax thresholds. These had not been adjusted
in the previous 14 years, despite significant wage growth. We also increased the in-work
tax credit, which helps low and middle income working families with children, and we
expanded eligibility for the independent earner tax credit. Working people in this country
4 Nov 2025 Oral Questions 13825
now get to keep more of the money that they work so hard to earn. That is reward for
effort, and it is delivered within tight Budget operating allowances. An estimated 727,000
households benefited by at least $75 a fortnight, and members opposite voted against it.

items.speaker: Cameron Brewer
items.text: What—[Interruption]

items.speaker: DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: Quiet during questions, please.

items.speaker: Cameron Brewer
items.text: What else has the Government done to encou rage effort and
investment through the tax system?

items.speaker: Hon SIMON WATTS
items.text: On behalf of the Minister of Finance, study after study has
identified that compared to other countries, New Zealand has a low level of capital
investment per worker. To raise productivity, lift incomes, and drive long-term economic
growth, New Zealand needs businesses, big and small, to invest in machinery, tools,
equipment, technology, vehicles, industrial buildings, and other capital assets. In this
year’s Budget, the G overnment launched Investment Boost, a tax incentive for New
Zealand businesses to make these sorts of capital investments. As a consequence of this
policy, we expect to see a lift in New Zealand’s capital stock, a lift in GDP, and a lift in
wages, again delivered within tight Budget operating allowances, and, again, opposed by
members on that side of the House.

items.speaker: DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: That answer was quite long enough. I’d like them to be a bit
briefer, please.

items.speaker: Cameron Brewer
items.text: What sort of tax would be ruled out by the Government’s revenue
strategy?

items.speaker: Hon SIMON WATTS
items.text: Well, on behalf of the Minister of Finance, it would be one
that, according to an Australian expert report —and I quote —“is a tax which in any
administrative form must be complex and difficult and produce some abnormalities and
inequalities of its own. There is no doubt whatsoever that any revenue it raises could be
more cheaply and easily raised in other ways.” In addition, if that tax discouraged effor t
and investment, such as an investment in small -business premises, and if it gave
preferential treatment to certain groups—for example, people that inherit property—

items.speaker: DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: No, I think that that’s a long enough answer. Thank you.
Question No. 3—

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: Madam Speaker.

items.speaker: DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: Sorry—the Rt Hon Winston Peters. Is this a supplementary or
a point of order?

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters

Can I ask the Minister, looking around the world, is there any comparative equality in

items.speaker: Hon Willie Jackson

items.speaker: DEPUTY SPEAKER

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters

you pay attention.

items.speaker: Hon Willie Jackson

education about taxation.

items.speaker: Hon Kieran McAnulty

items.speaker: DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: OK, I’ll just ask—I’ve got a point of order here from the Hon
Kieran McAnulty.

items.speaker: Hon Kieran McAnulty
items.text: With respect, Madam Speaker, the question should have been
ruled out by now. The minute that the Minister asked his colleague for opinions on a
Labour Party policy, that was out of order.
13826 Oral Questions 4 Nov 2025

items.speaker: DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: Yeah, the reason the question hasn’t been ruled out by now is
because there’s a lot of noise coming during supplementary questions. I’d like the Rt Hon
Winston Peters to ask that question again without referring to the Opposition and to ask
the question straight to the Minister, and the Opposition will be quiet.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: Having heard of a recent example of a limited capital gains
tax, is there anywhere in the world where an economy has adopted that policy?

items.speaker: Hon SIMON WATTS
items.text: On behalf of the Minister of Finance, what I am clear about—
and I am not aware of other countries in the world that are looking to punish their citizens
for success—

items.speaker: DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: No.

items.speaker: Hon SIMON WATTS
items.text: —through taxation, and that is exactly what that side of the
House—

items.speaker: DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: No, that’s not an answer. Sit down, please.

items.speaker: Hon Kieran McAnulty
items.text: Point of order, Madam Speaker. You made it extremely clear
to the member asking the question that it was not to be in reference to any other party’s
policy. The Minister then, in response, completely ignored your clear guidance.

items.speaker: DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: Well, I cut the Minister off and asked him to sit down because
I could see what was happening there.

items.speaker: Hon Kieran McAnulty
items.text: He didn’t, though, did he? He continued on.

items.speaker: DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: Well, no, he did. I said that that was enough and to finish off
the answer, and I asked him to sit down.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: With respect to tax policy, has the Minister heard the
statement “If you can’t stand the heat, get out of the kitchen”?

items.speaker: DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: No, that’s not a question. Thank you.
Question No. 3—Prime Minister
3. CHLÖE SWARBRICK (Co-Leader—Green) to the Prime Minister: E tautoko
ana ia i ngā kōrero me ngā mahi katoa a tōna Kāwanatanga?
[Does he stand by all of his Government’s statements and actions?]

items.speaker: Rt Hon CHRISTOPHER LUXON
items.text: Yes.
Chlöe Swarbrick: What is the effective tax rate paid by the wealthiest 1 percent of
New Zealanders, and why is it half the effective tax rate of the average hard-working New
Zealander?

items.speaker: Rt Hon CHRISTOPHER LUXON
items.text: We have a progres sive income tax system in
New Zealand, and the more money you earn, the more tax you pay.
Chlöe Swarbrick: How is it fair that hard-working New Zealanders pay tax on every
dollar they earn through income while the super-wealthy passively accumulate more and
more untaxed wealth without lifting a finger?

items.speaker: Rt Hon CHRISTOPHER LUXON
items.text: Well, in answer to the member’s first leg to that
question, it’s somewhat ironic because she and her party did not support basic tax reli ef
for low and middle income working New Zealanders. It wasn’t ideological; it was a pretty
simple up and down vote of “Do you lift the tax thresholds for low and middle income
working New Zealanders?”, and Labour, the Greens, and Te Pāti Māori all said no
because you do not care about working New Zealanders—period.

items.speaker: Hon Kieran McAnulty
items.text: Point of order, Madam Speaker. Speakers’ rulings are quite
clear that no Minister should bring parties that aren’t involved in the question into the
fray, and that Minister —the Prime Minister —does it repeatedly and has been told by
other presiding officers not to do it.

items.speaker: DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: Yep, thank you, and I’d ask the Prime Minister to refrain from
doing it for the rest of the day.

Question No. 5—Biosecurity
5. CAMERON LUXTON (ACT)  to the Minister for Biosecurity : What recent
announcements has he made about strengthening the biosecurity system?

items.speaker: Hon ANDREW HOGGARD
items.text: Last week, I announced
the Government’s plan for overhauling the Biosecurity Act to saf eguard New Zealand’s
primary sector into the future. As an island food -producing nation, our prosperity relies
on protection from biosecurity threats. New Zealand exports $60 billion of food and fibre
products each year, and our relative freedom from pests  and diseases is a big part of our
competitive advantage and underpins our primary sector. That’s why we’re modernising
the Biosecurity Act with nearly 50 proposals for change that will strengthen protection
against invasive pests and diseases.

items.speaker: Cameron Luxton
items.text: How could an invasive species or a disease that impacts animals
have such a big impact on our economy?

items.speaker: Hon Dr Ayesha Verrall
items.text: Oh, he’s really kicking the hornets’ nest now!

items.speaker: Hon ANDREW HOGGARD
items.text: Yes, and we’ll take care of them. The primary sector
really is the backbone of our economy, but we cannot afford to be complacent. Diseases
and invasive species can spread fast and wipe out entire sectors if they are not prevented
at the border or d etected early and managed properly. Economic analysis from the New
Zealand Institute of Economic Research says that a foot-and-mouth incursion would cost
over $14 billion a year. That wouldn’t just cost farmers; it would shut down our economy
and permanent ly damage our international reputation and credibility. Our biosecurity
system is strong, and we’re committed to maintaining a strong border and robust
biosecurity systems.

items.speaker: Cameron Luxton
items.text: How will the biosecurity system at the border be strengthened?

items.speaker: Hon ANDREW HOGGARD
items.text: One of the things we will be doing is to introduce a
new offence for not declaring high-risk goods such as raw meat at the border. This offence
will attract a fine of $800, while low -risk goods not dec lared will stay at $400. Our
relative freedom from pests and diseases is greatly valued by all Kiwis, and this will
remind visitors that New Zealand takes biosecurity seriously. We cannot afford to put our
primary sector and our natural environment at risk , and the best way to manage any
biosecurity incursion is to stop it from happening in the first place.

items.speaker: Cameron Luxton
items.text: What changes have been made to import health standards?
4 Nov 2025 Oral Questions 13831

items.speaker: Hon ANDREW HOGGARD
items.text: We’re improving New Zealand’s import rules by
making the development of import health standards more flexible and allowing risk
assessments to be tailored to the scenario—for example, we will enable the ability to issue
a one-off permit for goods where it wouldn’t make sense to develop and maintain an
import health standard. These changes are in addition to a new programme of work that I
announced this year, aimed at significantly reducing the time it takes to develop an import
health standard. This will enable higher volumes of trade, and thus give exporters greater
access to new materials to develop innovative products without lowering our biosecurity
standards.

items.text: On the matter of pests, can the Minister confirm what is the status

items.text: I believe in terms of where you’ve got a pest at a
regional level, the regional council does take precedence. But, yes, we will be looking to
equip Biosecurity New Zealand with lots of flamethrowers to try and remove that, and
spiders.
Question No. 6—Health
6. SAM UFFINDELL (National —Tauranga) to the Minister of Health : What
actions is the Government taking to increase vaccination rates?

items.speaker: Hon SIMEON BROWN
items.text: Our Government is taking the current
measles outbreak very seriously. Cases are now confirmed across multiple regions, and
the risk of continued transmission is high. That’s why, this week, Health New Zealand
has launched a nationwide Measles Immunisation Week, to highlight the need for Kiwis
to get immunised. Measles is a serious disease. In the 2019 outbreak, one in three people
who contracted measles needed hospital care. That’s why Health New Zealand is running
pop-up clinics, tracing contacts, and supporting families to lift our vaccination coverage
in order to stamp out the measles outbreak and to prevent the wider impacts of this disease
on our schools, our health system, society, and the economy.

items.speaker: Sam Uffindell
items.text: What steps has the Government taken to reduce the impact of serious
diseases like measles?

items.speaker: Hon SIMEON BROWN
items.text: We have reinstated the health target for immunisation, and
after years of decline, our latest quarterly health target results show that 82 percent of
children are now fully immunised by age two, up from 76.5 percent at 30 June last year,
representing the largest annual gain across all of our health targets. This shows that our
focus on targets is working. Whilst this is a significant increase, though, there is still much
more work to be done. Health New Zealand is working with providers to make it easier
for people to get their MMR vaccines and other vaccines, including through extra and
pop-up clinics, to prevent the outbreak from worsening.

items.speaker: Sam Uffindell
items.text: Why is it important to increase the MMR vaccination rate?

items.speaker: Hon SIMEON BROWN
items.text: Measles is one of the most infectious viruses in the world.
One case can infect 12 to 18 unvaccinated people, and if you’re not immunised and you’re
exposed, there’s a 90 percent chance that you will catch it. Vaccination is the single best
way to protect families, prevent community spread, and take pressure off our hospitals,
with two doses of the MMR vaccine providing about 99 percent protect ion. We need
around 95 percent coverage to stop future outbreaks and to stamp out the current
incursion. Over the last few years, rates fell. We are now turning that around, but there’s
still more work to do.

items.speaker: Sam Uffindell
items.text: Why did the Government reintroduce the immunisation target?
13832 Oral Questions 4 Nov 2025

items.speaker: Hon SIMEON BROWN
items.text: Let’s be clear: we’re committed to giving every child the
healthiest possible start to life. Targets matter because, ultimately, that helps to drive the
system to ensure that we can reach the targets needed to prevent outbreaks such as what
we are experiencing today. It also ensures that children get the protection they need when
they need it. Whilst New Zealand’s overall vaccination rates have improved, there is still
much more work to do. That’s why Health New Zealand is working with providers this
week and all weeks to continue —particularly this week, with Measles Immunisation
Week—to drive up immunisation rates and to promote the need for immunisation so that
we can act decisively to prevent this outbreak from spreading.

items.speaker: Hon Dr Ayesha Verrall
items.text: Is it correct that despite his Government’s performance
against the target, the number of susceptible people is estimated to increase by a thousand
a month and,  therefore, the risk of an outbreak continues to grow irrespective of the
target?

items.speaker: Hon SIMEON BROWN
items.text: Well, I would say to that member that it is critically
important that we focus on improving immunisation rates, and I would point out wha t
happened to immunisation rates during the previous six years under the Labour
Government, where they fell from around 92 percent of two -year-olds to around 75
percent of two-year-olds due to the removal of the target. We have reintroduced the target,
we are now focused on meeting it, and we acknowledge that there’s a lot more work to
do and we’re focused on doing it.

items.speaker: Hon David Seymour
items.text: What approach is the Government taking to school attendance
in the course of this outbreak —particularly during NCEA exams —and what advice has
the director-general issued to schools in relation to attendance and the outbreak?

items.speaker: Hon SIMEON BROWN
items.text: The Director -General of Health has provided very clear
advice that school students should continue to attend schools and exams, unless they are
identified as a close contact and aren’t immunised. It’s about making sure that we
continue to get our children the education that they need. Ultimately, though, the very
clear message is that whether it’s teachers or students, immunisation is the best protection
against measles. We’re encouraging everyone to take up that opportunity to get
immunised, and the latest data, which I have just received, shows that there were around
2,500 measles immunisations delivered yesterday—the highest number since 2019.

Question No. 8—Health
8. Hon Dr AYESHA VERRALL (Labour) to the Minister of Health: Does he stand
by his statement that “We want all New Zealanders to be able to see a GP when they need
one”; if so, is it acceptable that almost one in six New Zealanders cannot afford to go to
the doctor?

items.speaker: Hon SIMEON BROWN
items.text: In the context it was made, yes. Our
Government is committed to ensuring that all New Zealanders can access the care they
need when they need it. To do this, we’ve delivered the biggest ever fu nding boost for
GPs—$175 million this year alone —at an allowable fee increase of just 3 percent,
keeping costs stable and predictable. We know that the biggest barrier for patients today
is actually getting an appointment. In 2023 -24, 25.7 percent of adult s couldn’t see a GP
due to wait times, up from 11.6 percent in 2021 -22. That is why we are focused on
affordability and accessibility. We’re extending prescriptions to 12 months where safe,
saving patients up to $105 a year in GP fees; we’re strengthening the primary care
workforce; we’ve launched a 24/7 online GP care service for times when patients can’t
see their regular GP; and we continue to target support through subsidised GP visits for
community services card holders, and the Very Low Cost Access sc heme. All of this is
about putting patients first and making sure that every Kiwi can get in to see a doctor
when they need to.

items.speaker: Hon Dr Ayesha Verrall
items.text: Will he help the tradie who said to me that “I don’t go to the
doctor’s, because I can’t afford to. I earn $24 an hour.”, or is he not bothered by the fact

items.speaker: Hon SIMEON BROWN
items.text: Well, as the member will be aware, there is the community
services card scheme, which means that those people earning that amount of money are
able to pay a maximum of $20 co -payment, and, ultimately, that member’s policy is to
put a capital gains tax on property, on commercial buildings, and on KiwiSaver so that
people earning high incomes can go to the doctor for free.

items.speaker: Hon Dr Ayesha Verrall
items.text: Does he recognise that the cost of doctors visits is harming
patients like the woman who wrote to me that she’d self -treated her joint problem with

items.speaker: Hon SIMEON BROWN
items.text: What I’d say to that member is that the increased number
